slides.lead: Your baby is not bored. They are budgeting.
slides.sub: Seven-month-olds look away from what is too predictable, and from what is too surprising.

slides.head: The setup
slides.body:
At the University of Rochester, 7- and 8-month-olds watched animated boxes rise to reveal a toy, or nothing, in sequences with fixed odds.

Each sequence ran until the baby looked away for one full second. A model scored every event for how surprising it was, given everything the baby had seen so far.

slides.head: Where attention went
slides.caption: A U-shaped curve with a sweet spot near 1.25 bits of information. Not too simple, not too complex. Bar lengths are illustrative of the pattern, not the published values.

slides.head: The catch
slides.body:
Seventy-two babies, one lab, one task. The U-curve could have been an average of babies with different tastes.

It was not: the same curve holds within individual infants, it appeared again with sound sequences, and an independent lab has since shown infants steer attention toward what they can learn from.

slides.head: At home
slides.body:
When your baby turns away from the rattle, they may simply be finished with it. Attention goes where the information rate is just right.

Worth remembering before you run the same game an eleventh time, or swap it for something entirely new.
